"The effects of the coronavirus will weigh on economic activity in the near term and pose risks to the economic outlook." This language is clearly negative, emphasizing downside risks, declining market-based inflation compensation, and stress in the energy sector—consistent with literature linking adverse shocks to deflation risks and liquidity-trap conditions that can depress output (Svensson on inflation-forecast targeting; references noting “Economic Conditions associated with deflation” and “Economy can fall into Liquidity Trap”). However, the FOMC’s swift cut to the effective lower bound, large-scale purchases of Treasuries and agency MBS, expanded repo operations, discount-window ease, and dollar swap lines align with the “credit view” and financial-frictions literature showing that easing supports the flow of credit, lowers external finance premia, and stabilizes funding markets (Oliner and Rudebusch 1996a; Kashyap, Lamont, and Stein 1994; Gertler and Gilchrist 1994; references on bank capital, liquidity buffers, and the role of credit markets under imperfect information). Given these mitigating policy actions, the overall tone remains negative but less so than a purely risk-focused reading.
